items.text:
The process restore API is flawed because it only works for UI components.

Supporting process restore vs a fresh process start are two separate flows, but we are unable to differentiate those flows and restore state accordingly in `Application#onCreate()`.

Example: I might want to store some session information between process restore, but not on disk in permanent storage. How can I do that at the `Application#onCreate()` level?

Traditionally, the `ViewModel` is supposed to be a model (data class) for the view. Instead, Jetpack created an object whose job is to hold a view model (view state), but named it `ViewModel`.

A better name could have been `ViewModeler` or `ViewModelHolder`.

In reality, the Jetpack `ViewModel` is just a scoping mechanism to notify you when `onCleared()` is called.

Tooling around Groovy is hard because it's a dynamically typed language. Tooling around a statically typed language like Kotlin is much easier. That's why Kotlin makes so much sense for Gradle

What I really like about this article is that it clarifies ownership of the dispatcher.

It's not the UIs job to decide what dispatcher the function runs on.

```

```

The above function should internally specify `Dispatchers.Default`, and not rely on the caller to switch to the correct thread.

> 95 percent have said that they would be willing to accept slower builds if they could write their code in Kotlin.

Wow!

I would argue the issue isn't Kotlin, it's the lack of incremental builds due to annotation processing. Why is annotation processing so necessary?

Kotlin's built in features means you can forgo traditionally used annotation processing libs that you would use in Java (AutoValue, Dagger, etc). 

We started a new project last year, and are 100% Kotlin. We have explicitly forbid `kapt` and any annotation processing with a focus on incremental builds. Our devs are pretty happy with this choice.

I doubt that has much to do with it. I don't use Kotlin for CV or monetary purposes. I use it because it's simply more enjoyable to code in. As a developer, the Kotlin language allows me to express my ideas easier and better than the Java language.
I would attribute **most** build speed issues not to project size, but misuse of the build tools. Using Gradle without fully incremental builds is a recipe for frustration.
